title: The conditional
description: Ask politely, give advice, make wishes and imagine with “would”.

guide.summary: The conditional is how French says would. It turns a blunt demand into a polite request, an order into advice, and a fact into something only wished for or imagined.

sections.title: How do you build a conditional?
sections.text: Take the future stem — for most verbs the whole infinitive, minus the final e of an -re verb — and add the endings of the imparfait.
steps: Build the stem: the infinitive, minus the final e of an -re verb (prendre → prendr-).
Check the stem ends in r; every conditional form keeps it.
Find the subject and add its ending from the table.
watch: The r of the stem is never dropped: je parlais is the past, not “I would speak”.
-re verbs drop only the final e: prendr-, vendr-, dir- — never prendere-.
Verbs in -ger and -yer keep the full infinitive as a stem: voyager → voyagerais.

sections.title: The stems you have to learn
sections.text: These verbs have their own stem in the future, and the conditional uses exactly that stem. The endings are the ones in the first table.
steps: Before building a stem from the infinitive, check the verb against this list.
Take the stem from the table, then add the ending of your subject.
Falloir and pleuvoir exist only with il.

examples.en: I would be glad to come.
We would have to leave early.

watch: Never rebuild these on the infinitive: allerais, averions and devoirait do not exist.
Pouvoir, courir and voir have a double r: pourrais, courrais, verrais.
The stem is the same as in the future; only the ending tells the two tenses apart.

sections.title: Asking and offering politely
sections.text: In a shop, a hotel or an email the present sounds abrupt. Putting vouloir or pouvoir in the conditional makes the same sentence polite.
steps: Decide what is being asked: something you want (vouloir) or something the other person does (pouvoir).
Put that verb in the conditional for the right person.
Keep the rest of the sentence as it was — an inversion stays an inversion.

examples.fr: Je voudrais un café, s’il vous plaît.
examples.en: I would like a coffee, please.

watch: With vous the ending is -iez: pourriez-vous, never pourrais-vous.
The future (je voudrai, pourrez-vous) announces or predicts; it does not ask.
S’il vous plaît is a signal: the verb in front of it is usually in the conditional.

sections.title: Giving advice with devoir
sections.text: Devoir in the conditional means should. The verb after it stays in the infinitive.
steps: Put devoir in the conditional for the person you are advising.
Leave the following verb in the infinitive.
To soften an order, drop the imperative and start with the subject instead.
watch: Tu dois is an obligation (must); the conditional only suggests.
Never conjugate the second verb: it is tu devrais manger, not tu devrais manges.
Vous devrez is the future (will have to), not advice.

sections.title: Saying what you would like
sections.text: Aimer and vouloir in the conditional express a wish. An infinitive or a noun follows directly, with no preposition.
steps: Spot the wish: “would like”, not “like”.
Put aimer or vouloir in the conditional for the subject of the wish.
Attach the infinitive or the noun straight after, with no de.

examples.fr: Mes parents aimeraient vivre au bord de la mer.
examples.en: My parents would like to live by the sea.

watch: J’aime voyager states a taste; the conditional states a wish.
Bien often strengthens the wish and follows the verb: j’aimerais bien partir.
A wish is not a plan: the future says what you will do, not what you would like.

sections.title: Imagining a situation that is not real
sections.text: When the situation is invented rather than true, the verb goes into the conditional. A phrase at the front usually sets it up.

rows: Avec un jardin, nous ferions des barbecues.
Dans un monde idéal, tout le monde aurait une maison.
Si j’avais le temps, je viendrais.

steps: Find the phrase that makes the situation unreal: à ta place, avec…, sans…, dans un monde idéal, si + imparfait.
Put the main verb in the conditional, on its future stem.
After si itself, use the imparfait — never the conditional.

examples.en: If I were you, I would leave.

examples.fr: Sans téléphone, je serais plus calme.
examples.en: Without a phone I would be calmer.

watch: The conditional goes in the other half of a si sentence, never straight after si.
The present would claim the situation is true: avec un jardin, nous faisons… says you have one.
Tout le monde is singular in French: tout le monde aurait, not auraient.

sections.title: -ais, -rai or -rais?
sections.text: Three forms look alike. The r of the future stem separates the imparfait from the other two; the ending separates the future from the conditional.
steps: Is the sentence about the past? No r on the stem: that is the imparfait.
Is it certain, about what will happen? Future stem plus a short future ending.
Is it would — polite, advice, wish or imagined? Future stem plus an imparfait ending.

examples.fr: Demain, je te donnerai ma réponse.
examples.en: Tomorrow I will give you my answer.

examples.fr: Quand j’étais petit, je lisais beaucoup.
examples.en: When I was little, I read a lot.

examples.fr: À ta place, j’achèterais cette veste.
examples.en: In your place, I would buy this jacket.

watch: Je parlerai and je parlerais sound almost the same; only the spelling shows will or would.
With je, one letter changes everything: the future ends in -ai, the conditional in -ais.
-ait belongs to il and elle, never to je or tu.

Find the subject and add its imparfait ending.
Check the form has both the r of the stem and an ending among -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient.
Check the verb against the list of irregular stems before using the infinitive.
Take its stem from the table, then add the ending of the subject.
Remember the ending is the imparfait one, not the short future one.
Decide what is asked: what you want (vouloir) or what the other person does (pouvoir).
Put that verb in the conditional for the right person.
Keep the rest of the sentence, including any inversion, exactly as it was.
Put devoir in the conditional for the person you are advising.
Keep the verb that follows in the infinitive.
Match the ending to the subject: -ais for je and tu, -ait for il, -ions and -iez for nous and vous.
Check it is a wish (“would like”), not a statement of taste (“like”).
Put aimer or vouloir in the conditional for the subject.
Attach the infinitive or the noun directly, with no preposition.
Find the phrase that makes the situation unreal: à ta place, avec…, sans…, dans un monde idéal.
Put the main verb in the conditional, built on its future stem.
Check the ending against the subject of that verb.
Locate the sentence in time: past scene, certain future, or unreal situation?
No r on the stem means the imparfait.
With an r, choose the ending: the short future one for a certainty, the imparfait one for would.

alternatives.message: J’aimerai is the future (will). Would is the conditional, which ends in -rais, -rait, -rions, -riez or -raient.
Je voudrai is the future (will). Would is the conditional, which ends in -rais, -rait, -rions, -riez or -raient.

exercises.hint: Would like is aimer or vouloir in the conditional.
exercises.feedback: Use the conditional, ending in -ais for je.
exercises.explanation: J’aimerais and je voudrais both express a wish in the conditional.

mistakes.why: Those are the present: “I like travelling” and “I want to travel”. Would like is softer and needs the conditional.
Aimais is the imparfait: it talks about a past habit, not about a wish.
The ending -ait is for il and elle, but the subject is je.
After vouloir and aimer the infinitive follows directly, with no preposition.

exercises.instruction: Turn this into a wish: put aimer in the conditional.
exercises.hint: Future stem of aimer plus the elle ending of the imparfait.
exercises.feedback: Change aime into the conditional.
exercises.explanation: Aimer- + -ait gives elle aimerait, she would like.

mistakes.why: This is still the present: it reports what she likes. A wish needs the conditional.
Aimera is the future: “she will like”. A wish takes an imparfait ending on that stem.
The ending -ais goes with je and tu, and the subject is elle.
Aimait is the imparfait: it says what she used to like, with no r on the stem.

exercises.hint: Look at the ending of the verb and at the subject.
exercises.feedback: This is a wish, and the ending does not match tu.
exercises.explanation: With tu, the conditional ends in -ais: tu aimerais.

mistakes.why: The ending -ai is the je form of the future. With tu the conditional takes the ending it shares with the imparfait.
Aimeras is the future: “will you like”. The question is a tentative invitation, so it needs the conditional.
Aimais is the imparfait: it asks about the past instead of about a wish.
The ending -ait is for il and elle. The subject here is tu.

exercises.source: À ta place, je ____ ce travail.
exercises.hint: À ta place describes something imagined. Check the ending for je.
exercises.feedback: An imagined situation uses the conditional.
exercises.explanation: À ta place calls for the conditional: je prendrais.

mistakes.why: That is the future: “I will take”. À ta place imagines a situation that is not real.
Prenais is the imparfait: “I was taking”. The r of the future stem is missing.
The ending -ait is for il and elle. The speaker here is je.

exercises.source: Dans un monde idéal, tout le monde ____ (avoir) une maison.
exercises.hint: Tout le monde takes the il form. Avoir has an irregular stem.
exercises.feedback: An imagined world calls for the conditional of avoir.
exercises.explanation: Aur- + -ait gives tout le monde aurait.

mistakes.why: Aura is the future: “everyone will have”. Dans un monde idéal is imaginary, so the ending must be an imparfait one.
Avait is the imparfait: it describes the past, and it lacks the r of the future stem.
Tout le monde sounds plural in English but takes the il form in French, so the ending stays singular.
The ending -ais goes with je and tu, and this subject is third person.
A is the present: it claims the world already is like that.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French. Start with À ta place.
exercises.source: If I were you (to a friend), I would leave (partir).

alternatives.message: Je partirai is the future (will). Would is the conditional, which ends in -rais, -rait, -rions, -riez or -raient.

exercises.hint: The situation is imagined, so the verb is in the conditional.
exercises.feedback: Use the conditional of partir with je.
exercises.explanation: À ta place, je partirais: partir- + -ais.

mistakes.why: Pars is the present: it says you are leaving now. The sentence imagines being someone else.
Partais is the imparfait, about the past, and it has no r on the stem.
Votre is the formal possessive. The instruction says you are speaking to a friend.
The ending -ait is for il and elle, but the subject is je.

exercises.instruction: Put the verb in the conditional to show it is only imagined.
exercises.source: Avec un jardin, nous faisons des barbecues.
answers: Avec un jardin, nous ferions des barbecues.
exercises.hint: Faire has an irregular stem in the conditional.
exercises.feedback: Use the future stem of faire with the nous ending of the imparfait.
exercises.explanation: Fer- + -ions gives nous ferions: we would have barbecues.

answers: Avec un jardin, nous faisons des barbecues.
mistakes.why: Faisons is the present: it claims you really do have barbecues. The garden is only imagined.

answers: Avec un jardin, nous ferons des barbecues.
mistakes.why: Ferons is the future: “we will have”. The garden is imaginary, so an imparfait ending belongs on that stem.

answers: Avec un jardin, nous faisions des barbecues.
mistakes.why: Faisions is the imparfait: it tells what you used to do, and it has no r.

answers: Avec un jardin, nous fairions des barbecues.
mistakes.why: Faire does not keep its infinitive as a stem; its stem is short and irregular.

exercises.instruction: Fix the verb: this situation is only imagined.
exercises.source: Sans téléphone, je serai plus calme.
answers: Sans téléphone, je serais plus calme.
exercises.hint: An imagined situation needs would, not will.
exercises.feedback: Serai is the future.
exercises.explanation: Would be is the conditional: je serais.

answers: Sans téléphone, je serai plus calme.
mistakes.why: That ending is the future: it promises this will really happen. Sans téléphone only imagines a situation.

answers: Sans téléphone, je suis plus calme.
mistakes.why: Suis is the present: it states a fact about now, not something imagined.
Étais is the imparfait, about the past. The sentence imagines a situation instead.

answers: Sans téléphone, je serait plus calme.
mistakes.why: The ending -ait is for il and elle. The subject here is je.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence in the conditional.
exercises.source: In his place, she would say no.
answers: À sa place, elle dirait non.
exercises.hint: Two tiles are forms of dire. Only one is the conditional.
exercises.feedback: Dira is the future. Would is the conditional.
exercises.explanation: Dir- + -ait gives elle dirait.

answers: À sa place, elle dira non.
mistakes.why: Dira is the future: “she will say”. Being in his place is imagined, not something that will happen.

exercises.source: Je te le promets : demain, je te ____ ma réponse.
exercises.hint: A promise about tomorrow says what will happen.
exercises.feedback: This is a certain future event, not an imagined one.
exercises.explanation: Will give is the future: je donnerai. Donnerais would mean would give.

mistakes.why: That is the conditional: “I would give”. A promise about tomorrow states something certain, not something imagined.
Donnais is the imparfait: “I used to give”. It points to the past, but demain points forward.

exercises.hint: Quand j’étais petit describes a past habit.
exercises.feedback: A past habit uses the imparfait, which has no r of the future stem.
exercises.explanation: Used to read is the imparfait: je lisais.

mistakes.why: The r marks the future stem and the ending marks would: “I would read”. Quand j’étais petit reports what really happened.
That is the future: “I will read”. The sentence is set in childhood, in the past.

exercises.instruction: Change the future into the conditional.
exercises.source: Avec ton aide, je finirai ce soir.
answers: Avec ton aide, je finirais ce soir.
exercises.hint: Keep the stem and change only the ending.
exercises.feedback: The conditional has the future stem plus the imparfait ending.
exercises.explanation: Je finirai (will) becomes je finirais (would): the ending -ai becomes -ais.

answers: Avec ton aide, je finirai ce soir.
mistakes.why: That ending is the future: the sentence still says the work will really be done.

answers: Avec ton aide, je finissais ce soir.
mistakes.why: Finissais is the imparfait: it drops the r of the future stem and moves the sentence into the past.

answers: Avec ton aide, je finirait ce soir.
mistakes.why: The ending -ait is for il and elle, but the subject is je.

answers: Avec ton aide, je finirions ce soir.
mistakes.why: The ending -ions goes with nous. Only the ending for je had to change.

exercises.instruction: Write pleuvoir in the right tense: imparfait, future or conditional.
exercises.source: Hier, il ____ (pleuvoir) quand je suis sorti.
exercises.hint: Hier sets a background scene in the past, behind je suis sorti.
exercises.feedback: The scene is in the past, so neither the future stem nor the conditional fits.
exercises.explanation: A past background uses the imparfait: il pleuvait.

mistakes.why: Pleuvra is the future: “it will rain”. Hier puts the whole scene in the past.
That is the conditional: “it would rain”. Nothing is imagined here — the rain was really falling.
A plu is the passé composé, which reports one finished event. Behind je suis sorti you need the background scene.
Pleut is the present: it describes now, but the sentence says hier.

exercises.instruction: Fix the verb: this situation is only imagined.
exercises.source: À ta place, j’achèterai cette veste.
answers: À ta place, j’achèterais cette veste.
exercises.hint: À ta place needs would, not will.
exercises.feedback: J’achèterai is the future.
exercises.explanation: Would buy is the conditional: j’achèterais.

answers: À ta place, j’achèterai cette veste.
mistakes.why: That ending is the future: it says you really will buy the jacket. À ta place imagines being someone else.

answers: À ta place, j’achetais cette veste.
mistakes.why: Achetais is the imparfait: it reports a past habit and has no r on the stem.

answers: À ta place, j’achèterait cette veste.
mistakes.why: The ending -ait is for il and elle, but the subject is j’.

answers: À ta place, j’achète cette veste.
mistakes.why: Achète is the present: it states what you really do, not what you would do in someone else’s place.

alternatives.message: Je viendrai is the future (will). Would is the conditional, which ends in -rais, -rait, -rions, -riez or -raient.

exercises.hint: Would is the conditional: irregular stem of venir plus the je ending.
exercises.feedback: Check the ending: would needs -rais.
exercises.explanation: Viendr- + -ais gives je viendrais.

mistakes.why: Viens is the present: it says you are coming. Would come is more tentative.
Venais is the imparfait, about the past, and it lacks the r of the future stem.
The ending -ait is for il and elle. The subject is je.
Venir does not keep its infinitive as a stem; its stem is irregular and contains a d.
That ending is the future: “I will come”. Would needs the imparfait ending on the same stem.
